extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of history, literature, philosophy, and moral/political theory (general educated public)
extracted.subtask_description: Lectures/essay (Thomas Carlyle) that analyzes the nature, forms, and effects of 'Heroes' and 'Hero-worship' across history, classifying types and arguing for the centrality of great men to Universal History. Useful for thinking about qualities, social role, and interpretation of great figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion as the chief fact about a man
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is well said, in every sense, that a man's religion is the chief fact with regard to him."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle defines 'religion' not as formal creed but as the thing a man 'does practically believe'—the practical conviction about his relation to the Unseen that creatively determines his thoughts and actions. He instructs readers to ask first what religion (Heathenism, Christianism, Scepticism, etc.) a man or nation has, because answering that gives 'the soul of the history of the man or nation.' This is a primary evaluative criterion for understanding a Great Man.

rubrics_metrics.name: Great Men as the soul/agents of Universal History
rubrics_metrics.description: "Universal History, the history of what man has accomplished in this world, is at bottom the History of the Great Men who have worked here."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate historical accomplishment by locating the Great Men who modelled and created social facts: their thoughts parented actions; public achievements are embodiments of ideas that dwelt in great men. Carlyle treats biography of Great Men as the key to understanding epochs and changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hero-worship as a formative social principle
rubrics_metrics.description: "Hero-worship... is the grand modifying element in that ancient system of thought... Society is founded on Hero-worship."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle treats admiration, reverence, submission and loyalty toward great men as the basis of social order and hierarchy ('Heroarchy'). When genuine, such worship vivifies society; when substituted by false or 'forged' leaders, it produces decay and revolution. Thus the presence, form, and authenticity of hero-worship is a criterion for assessing social health and legitimacy of authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of a Hero: original insight, manhood, and heroic nobleness
rubrics_metrics.description: "He is the living light-fountain... of native original insight, of manhood and heroic nobleness;--in whose radiance all souls feel that it is well with them."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle emphasizes personal traits to identify a Hero: originality of insight, moral/heroic nobility, and the power to illumine others. Proximity to such a person benefits others; these character traits are ways to evaluate an individual's greatness beyond formal titles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Great Man as indispensable savior of an epoch (wisdom and valor)
rubrics_metrics.description: "In all epochs of the world's history, we shall find the Great Man to have been the indispensable savior of his epoch;--the lightning, without which the fuel never would have burnt."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A decisive criterion is the individual's capacity to discern what an age requires (wisdom) and to lead courageously (valor). Carlyle rejects the reductionist view that 'the Time made the man' and instead argues that certain times require a great man to avoid ruin; success in this salvific role is evidence of true greatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of Hero types (six classes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contents list: "THE HERO AS DIVINITY. ODIN. PAGANISM: SCANDINAVIAN MYTHOLOGY. / THE HERO AS PROPHET. MAHOMET: ISLAM. / THE HERO AS POET. DANTE: SHAKSPEARE. / THE HERO AS PRIEST. LUTHER; REFORMATION: KNOX; PURITANISM. / THE HERO AS MAN OF LETTERS. JOHNSON, ROUSSEAU, BURNS. / THE HERO AS KING. CROMWELL, NAPOLEON: MODERN REVOLUTIONISM."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle proposes a typology of heroes (divinity, prophet, poet, priest, man of letters, king) as distinct modes by which greatness appears and functions. Use this taxonomy to classify and evaluate the mode of a given historical figure and the sort of authority or influence they exercise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject explanations that reduce religions to quackery or mere allegory
rubrics_metrics.description: "Some speculators have a short way of accounting for the Pagan religion: mere quackery, priestcraft, and dupery, say they... Another theory... attributes such things to Allegory... I find... they have not reached it either."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological injunction: when interpreting religious/heroic phenomena, avoid simplistic dismissals (quackery) or claiming they were only poetic allegory that produced belief. Carlyle argues that religions and hero-worship contained a 'kind of fact at the heart of them'—earnest truths that motivated real convictions—so evaluators should seek the substantive beliefs and functions rather than reduce them to fraud or mere symbolism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impersonation/personification of natural forces in Pagan heroism
rubrics_metrics.description: "The primary characteristic of this old Northland Mythology I find to be Impersonation of the visible workings of Nature."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle treats the personification of natural phenomena (Jotuns, Thor, Balder, Aegir, etc.) as a sincere cognitive and emotional response: the forces of nature were seen as godlike personal agencies. When evaluating ancient hero/heroic-religious systems, consider how personification functioned to make the world intelligible and awe-inspiring to people, and assess the 'fibre of truth' in those responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worship as transcendent wonder; man as the visible Shekinah
rubrics_metrics.description: "Worship is transcendent wonder... 'The true Shekinah is Man!'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle holds that worship springs from awe at the wonder of existence, and that man himself is the principal revelation of the Highest. Admiration of a great man is thus akin to reverence of what is divine in humanity. Use this as a criterion: a Hero's claim to reverence is strengthened when they embody and reveal what is highest in human nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endurance of hero-worship despite sceptical ages; admiration is inborn
rubrics_metrics.description: "In no time whatever can they entirely eradicate out of living men's hearts a certain altogether peculiar reverence for Great Men... Hero-worship endures forever while man endures."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle argues that even in skeptical, critical eras, an inborn tendency to revere greatness persists and serves as a social cornerstone ('everlasting adamant'). In evaluating modern or skeptical societies, note the persistence, transformation, or perversion of hero-worship as an index of cultural continuity or decay.
